name: Personal & Professional Development
description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
profile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives

description2: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.

description2: This course develops practical financial decision-making skills through case studies and real-world applications. Students learn to analyze financial data, assess risks, and make informed investment, budgeting, and business decisions that enhance value, financial security, and long-term planning.

name: Introduction to Economics
description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
profile: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
topics: game theory; theory of consumer behaviour; theory of the firm; market structure; aggregate output; inflation rate

name: Public Economics
description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
profile: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.
topics: market failure; public goods; p ublic spending; political economy; affect societal welfare; policies affect societal

name: Econometrics
description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
profile: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

methods: Econometrics; Regression analysis; Instrumental variables; Hypothesis testing; Monte Carlo simulation; Stata

name: Consumer Product Design
description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
profile: In this course you will learn how to function in a 'real-world' design and development environment. Hence, you will work in a group that mimics a design and development (d&d) team as e.g. in industry. The members of a team in this course fulfill roles similarly as occur in industrial d&d teams (e.g. chair person, secretary, ...). A team is responsible for much of its own planning. The functioning of a team involves e.g. preparing agendas for team meetings, taking minutes, planning practical work, maintaining a documentation system, etc. During the course, the instructor will NOT act as chairperson / team leader, but rather as an ‘external consultant'. During the course we will go through the various phases of the development of a consumer product: assessment of customer needs and translating these into a product concept, develop a method to make a product, both on laboratory- as on industrial scale, analyzing environmental impact, analyzing costs and proceeds. In a d&d project and hence in the course, activities are quite varied, and include interviewing potential customers, laboratory experiments, constructing quantitative mathematical model(s) of the working mechanism(s) of a product, constructing a prototype, work out how a product can be produced on an industrial scale, consider protection of intellectual property etc.. In this course, in addition to the more traditional aspects of the d&d process, special attention will be given to sustainability. This involves e.g. the nature of the materials used (natural, recycled, …), lifespan, repairability, 'circularity' etc.
topics: involves interviewing customers; probe customer needs; product; quantitative modeling; fabrication method; consumer

name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
description2: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
profile: Grounded in academic theory, real-world applications, and case studies, this course unpacks what drives consumers’ behaviour and engagement with brands, and how marketers can build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key concepts related to marketing strategy and consumer psychology and examines external forces influencing reinvention of the Marketing function, including digital and AI-driven marketing. Drawing on the work of Kotler, Aaker, Kapferer and other leading scholars, students will explore real-life case studies, develop marketing plans and learn how to create effective brand strategies for greater consumer engagement.
topics: ai-driven marketing; technology-driven marketing innovation; consumer engagement; customer trust responsibly; strategic marketing plan; sustainable brand strategies

name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
description2: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.

Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.

It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
profile: In this course, you will develop a new venture idea from the ground up. No prior business experience is required – working in teams you will learn by doing, developing a startup concept from ideation through to the final pitch. Along the way, you will gain essential business and entrepreneurial skills, including design thinking, market validation and business planning. This course fosters creativity, business acumen and collaboration to drive business and social entrepreneurship.
topics: design thinking; market validation; business planning; class fosters creativity; prior business expertise; final pitch

name: Research Methods & Statistics
description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
profile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
topics: research design; operationalization; sampling; experiments; surveys; descriptive and inferential statistics
methods: Research design; Operationalization; Experimental design; Survey research; Sampling; Descriptive statistics; Inferential statistics; ANOVA

name: Personal Leadership
description2: Personal Leadership provides a comprehensive introduction to leadership theory and practice, designed to help students discover their unique leadership style through self-awareness and practical skill-building. Through interactive workshops, reflective exercises, and real-world applications, students engage deeply with core leadership principles and develop the tools needed to lead confidently in any setting.
profile: Personal Leadership is an interactive course for Liberal Arts and Sciences students that introduces leadership fundamentals with a focus on self-awareness and practical skills. Through a blend of theory, interaction, and assessments, students will cultivate the tools needed to lead effectively in both personal and professional contexts. The course begins by exploring leadership fundamentals, emphasizing transformational leadership (Bass, 1990) and authentic leadership (Gardner et al., 2021), supported by foundational concepts from Northouse’s Leadership: Theory and Practice (2025), which offers a balanced overview of various leadership models and their applications. Covey’s (2020) The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: 30th Anniversary Edition provides a foundation for principles such as proactive behavior, prioritization, and fostering collaboration. Students critically analyze these concepts through evolutionary perspectives on adaptive strategies (Lonati & Van Vugt, 2023) and apply Locke and Latham’s (2019) goal-setting theory to develop actionable leadership plans. Self-awareness and emotional intelligence (Goleman, 2021) are central themes, with students engaging in reflective exercises, group discussions, and personality assessments to better understand their strengths, values, and leadership styles. The course maximizes interaction through workshops, group projects, role-playing, and peer feedback sessions, ensuring active engagement and collaboration.
topics: proactive behavior; fostering collaboration; unique leadership style; personal leadership; core leadership principles; lead confidently

name: Leadership Communication
description2: This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world, helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams, sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.
profile: Communication and leadership are two sides of the same coin; Quintilian, the famous Roman Professor of Rhetoric, knew this when he famously declared that the best leader is ‘the good person speaking well’. At the start of this course, the participants will be introduced the main leadership and communication models and theories. They will also read leading articles from the Harvard Business Review on leadership communication. Theories that will be explored will include transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership approaches. We will also explore the roles of gender, ethics and culture in communicative leadership positions. The module will focus on the role of emotional intelligence in communicating leadership; touching on key matters such as empathy, ethics, self-awareness and self-regulation. The course will also have a distinctive liberal arts and sciences flavour to it, analysing the leadership qualities and deficiencies of characters in prose fiction, film and drama. It is especially in the worlds created by Shakespeare, where key lessons about how to lead, and how not to lead, can be learned by the leaders of tomorrow. The course will also bring in real leaders from outside the college, from both the business and public sectors, to interact with the students on the subject matter of their own communicative leadership experiences and goals. Such interactions with entrepreneurial and industry heads may lead to spin-off internships in the following academic year.
topics: inspire teams; essential leadership; blends theory; communication; sharpen; helping

name: Leadership & Diversity Management
description2: Leadership & Diversity Management explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective leadership in dynamic, varied environments. Blending cutting-edge theories with hands-on practice, students develop the skills to lead with empathy, inclusivity, and adaptability. Through engaging case studies, interactive workshops, and reflective assessments, participants build awareness of diversity and learn to inspire ethical, collaborative teams.
profile: Leadership & Diversity Management explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective leadership in dynamic, varied environments. Blending cutting-edge theories with hands-on practice, students develop the skills to lead with empathy, inclusivity, and adaptability. Through engaging case studies, interactive workshops, and reflective assessments, participants build awareness of diversity and learn to inspire ethical, collaborative teams.
topics: leadership diversity management; blending cutting-edge theories; experiences shape effective; shape effective leadership; reflective assessments; collaborative teams

name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
description2: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
profile: People are the organisation. Without people, organisations cannot survive or be productive. This course, tailored for Liberal Arts and Sciences bachelor students, offers an interdisciplinary exploration of the psychological, social, and structural dynamics within organisations. It equips students with the knowledge and skills needed to navigate and influence organisational environments effectively throughout their academic and professional careers. Drawing on foundational and contemporary research in organisational behaviour, this upper- level undergraduate course incorporates a case-based approach that includes conceptual frameworks, case discussions, and skill-building activities. Students will explore topics such as motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and organizational culture using Robbins and Judge’s (2023) Organisational Behaviour as a primary resource. Additional literature and materials will supplement the course to provide a well-rounded perspective. Topics Covered => Core Concepts: Diversity in organisations, attitudes and job satisfaction, emotions and moods, personality and values, perception and decision-making, motivation, communication, leadership, power and politics, and conflict and negotiation. Structural Dynamics: The structure and culture of organisations, group behaviour, work teams, and organisational change. These topics are structured within a comprehensive model that defines the field of organisational behaviour and outlines its key concepts and relationships.
topics: organizational behavior; motivation; leadership; group dynamics; organizational culture; decision-making

name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
description2: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.
profile: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence; whether in business, leadership, or life. The course offers an immersive, practice-driven exploration of negotiation as both an analytical discipline and a strategic interpersonal skill. Students will engage in frequent simulations, role-plays, and reflective exercises designed to build confidence and adaptability into the dynamics that shape successful agreements. The course introduces the foundational theories and frameworks that define modern negotiation practice, including BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement), ZOPA analysis (zone of possible agreement), interest-based negotiation, and the dual-concern model. There will also be a focus on (i) avoiding bargaining over positions, (ii) separating people from the problem, (iii) focusing on interests not positions, (iv) inventing options for mutual gain, and (v) insisting on using objective criteria. Students will learn to diagnose negotiation structures, identify value-creation opportunities, and strategically manage trade-offs (e.g. logrolling). Core concepts such as anchoring, framing, concession patterns, and the psychology of influence will be woven throughout weekly activities. Because negotiation is inseparable from human behavior, the course integrates research from social psychology and language & communication studies.
topics: batna (best alternative to a negotiated agreement); zopa analysis (zone of possible agreement); interest-based negotiation; dual-concern model; concession patterns; craft persuasive arguments

name: Database Management Systems
description2: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
profile: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
topics: relational database theory; query processing; database management systems; relational database management; covers relational database; normalization

name: Introduction to Data Science
description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
profile: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
topics: spatial data; text data; data visualization; datasets; cleaning; manipulation

name: Machine Learning
description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
profile: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.
topics: linear regression; resampling methods; shrinkage approaches; tree - based methods; support vector machines; advanced tree based

name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
profile: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E).
topics: computer vision; large language models; generative ai; text classification; discuss recent developments; neural networks

name: Mathematical Methods
description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
profile: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3
topics: various techniques for integration; complex numbers; differential equations; solve equations; problem solving; linear algebra

name: Law, Society & Justice
description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
profile: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
topics: property law; torts law; moot court session; international legal organisations; legal traditions; socio scientific

name: Modern History
description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
profile: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations.
topics: national self determination; popular sovereignty; chronological overview; covers major economic; cultural developments; history

name: Histories of Gender
description2: Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
profile: This course explores the histories and lives of children and young and older adults, through the lens of gender within an American context. The education takes place in a safe environment where critical thought thrives. The time frame is the 19th through the 21st centuries. Thematic topics unfold within a chronological framework. They include slavery in the nineteenth century, surviving and thriving in the twentieth century, and individual and community activism today. The approach centers storytelling. Throughout the term we explore the significance of the ways gendered stories are told by i.e., educational institutions, in children’s storybooks, within the medical community, across social media, through cultural expressions and forms, and by individual people. For instance, class members conduct interviews of elderly Queer folks and interpret their findings by drawing from scholars including bell hooks and Kimberle Crenshaw. They also contribute to the semester long Walking with Pride Project, an activist artwork woven by students, Queer and multiply marginalized people world-wide, and their allies. The rug features digitally in https://thewalkingwithprideproject.wordpress.com/, and physically in cultural spaces internationally. Finally, students explore repression, resistance, and/or retribution in their final project, where they choose both the content of their research, ranging from transphobia to banned books, as well as the form, including but not limited to, an essay, podcast, graphic novel, or artistic expression.
topics: bell hooks; kimberle crenshaw; but not limited to; graphic novel; or artistic expression; queer cinema

name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
profile: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.
topics: human rights; french declaration; rights treaties; modern philosophers; traces; classical

name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
profile: In the course Introduction to Political Philosophy we shall examine the views on the nature of man, of society, and of political authority held by a number of influential Western thinkers. By the means of their particular political theories, the thinkers in question certainly intended to contribute to the solution of problems affecting the communities they were part of and their time. We shall look at the intellectual presuppositions of their theories and compare the problems they intended to solve, as well as their solutions, with the most significant actual political problems, the perception the general public opinion has of them and our current solutions. In particular, we shall focus on the authors’ justification for the existence and organization of political power. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the nature, characters, and purposes of each of the various political theories examined, from classical antiquity to today. To achieve this goal it is designed as informative and critical. Students are expected to master a number of relevant items and to assess form and quality of the influence that certain political theories have had, and may still have, on present day politics. In the attempt to determine whether there are ‘perennial’ political problems and features, students are expected to constantly compare past and present, and to find out what are the possible connections between empirical and normative political science.
topics: political philosophy; emphasises essay writing; contemporary texts; presentations; poverty; pluralism

name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
profile: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
topics: decline of political parties; impact of globalization; non majoritarian institutions; phenomena like democratic; like democratic backsliding; compare political systems

name: Introduction to Sociology
description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
profile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.

name: Qualitative Research Methodology
description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
profile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
topics: qualitative research methodology; conducting small team; interpreting meaning; power dynamics; reflecting; covers designing

name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
profile: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
topics: in ‘gossoci101 introduction to sociology’; ‘gossoci202 modern sociology’; social capital; social trust; civil sphere; civil repair in modern societies

name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
profile: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
profile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
topics: multivariate statistics; linear regression; factor analysis; ANOVA/ANCOVA; logistic regression; non-parametric tests
methods: Multivariate statistics; Regression analysis; Factor analysis; ANOVA/ANCOVA; Logistic regression; Non-parametric tests

name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
profile: How do we become unique individuals? Which factors influence this process and how do they interplay in each stage of our development during our lives? In this course we will explore these and many other questions about human development, where students will acquire knowledge and develop critical thinking and understanding of the main aspects related to human development throughout the lifespan. The main goal of the course Developmental Psychology is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and me thods in the field, which is concerned with human physical, cognitive, social and emotional development throughout the lifespan: from pregnancy to infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age; their descriptions and understandings, as well as t he most relevant theoretical approaches and some psychological assessment and interventions in the different phases of life. Therefore, this course will address the following subject areas: 1. Historical and contemporary views, and main theories in Developmental Psychology; 2. Biological and environmental foundations of human development; 3. Pre-natal development and birth; 4. Attachment and physical, cognitive, emotional and social development in infancy. 5. Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and personality development in early and middle childhood, adolescence and early, middle and late adulthood; 6. End of life: death, dying, and bereavement.
topics: human development; lifespan development; cognitive development; social development; aging

name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
profile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. name: Rhetoric in Action
description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
profile: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
topics: primary school children; local primary school; persuasive speaking; rhetorical theory; voices; public-speaking

name: Persuasive Communication
description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
profile: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
topics: persuasion; framing; nudging; cognitive shortcuts; ethics of persuasion; climate communication

name: Media & Race
description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
profile: Whose stories are remembered and whose are erased? What do the stories un/told teach us about power, privilege, and resistance? How do cultural expressions and forms like film, photographs, and music address systemic racism, critique the present, and envision just futures? These questions steer this course. Addressing them reveals links between past and present that students explore in final podcasts grounded in research and fueled by passion. Race, at the heart of American history and life, is at the center of this class. We begin in the late 19th century with the “end” of slavery and continue into the 21st century with the advent of ICE. Throughout the term we explore the ways media supports systems of oppression and empowers the oppressed.
discipline: Media Studies; Race and Ethnicity Studies
topics: creating podcasts; systemic racism; investigates storytelling; afrofuturism; links; relation
